messages.subject: Stratification?
messages.body_plain:
This problem, we have been struggling for the last few days, without much success. Kindly help.

Let us take an example of species X in the study site.
Let the site be divided into three strata, viz. Open Forest, Moderate Forest and Dense Forest.

We have total of nine transects, three eventually laid in each stratum.

Our idea is to obtain results with minimum CV (say about 10-20) and project results for long term monitoring. Logistics and changing encounter rate, visibility and weather are important constraints in increasing the number of spatial replicates.

Now we know that the species X is rarely found in Open Forest stratum, and populates the Dense Forest stratum well. What shall be our approach in order to obtain reliable results. We know that stratum Open Forest has very little of species X, but have to sample that area for this species for the sake of extrapolating results to the whole study site.

I made a querry regarding the same issue a few days ago and found replies promptly regarding keeping the number of samples to 9 instead of 1 (all lengths pooled). But what happens to the results in case of heterogenous habitats of a study site. Is there a method to reduce that CV which probably inflates due to the samples laid in "Open Forest" stratum (no or very less distribution of target species). What shall we do to further make our study design more efficient ?

I tried post stratifying the analysis and found the following CVs of the three different strata:
1.    Dense Forest:    CV = 16.53 %     ; # observations = 99
2.    Moderate Forest:    CV = 47.08 %    ; # observations = 107
3.    Open Forest:    CV = 139.48 %    ; # observations = 6

Do these CVs have something to do with possible improper stratification? Will restratification by dividing lines into different strata help in some cases where a particular transect line runs through various strata? What shall be the number of samples in this case. Our 9 transects (spatial replicates) were walked 12 times each (temporal replicates). If I am not mistaken, variance for estimation of CVs is calculated with help of encounter rates on individual sample (line)  and overall encounter rates.

Looking forward to some help.

Koustubh Sharma
INDIA.

messages.subject: Re: Stratification?
messages.body_plain:
Koustubh, your high cv's have nothing to do with improper stratification,
the problem is the lack of spatial replication - coupled with the small
number of detections in one stratum.  If you can't have more, shorter
lines, then I would not stratify - I would put your 9 lines randomly
distributed throughout the study area (or more likely,
systematically-spaced lines, with the grid of lines randomly located).
The heterogeneity in density does not invalidate your abundance estimate.
You are right that in principle, stratification should improve your
precision, but you simply don't have sufficient replication in space to
stratify.  Even without any stratification, you don't really have
sufficient replication in space, with just 9 lines.

Different detectability in your different strata won't bias
your estimate of abundance for the entire study area, due to the pooling
robustness property of line transect estimators, though if you calculate
separate estimates for each forest type, having used pooled data to
estimate the detection function, these are likely to be
biased.  (e.g. animals are likely to be more detectable in open forest, so
you will underestimate effective strip width in this stratum by pooling
data, and hence overestimate abundance in this stratum.)

Steve

messages.subject: Re: Stratification?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Koustubh, List,

3 lines per stratum is far too few for reliable estimation of variation in
encounter rate.  Indeed 9 lines is rather too few even ignoring the
stratification.  I think you should focus your survey effort on getting more
(possibly shorter) lines.  You will probably also have to reduce the temporal
replication to achieve this.

Section 7.2.1 of Introduction to Distance Sampling discusses transect layout,
and warns against the dangers of overstratification.  It may seem intuitive to
stratify effort so that you put more effort per unit area into high density
strata (see section 7.2.2.3), but if you end up with some strata with very few
lines in them you loose reliability.  Since you are going to struggle to have
enough lines per stratum for reliable estimation of encounter rate, and you are
also going to struggle to have enough observations in your low density stratum
to estimate detection function separately for that stratum, I suggest you use
the same allocation of effort per unit area for all 3 strata (in other words
same number of lines per unit area).  That way you can combine the strata
together at the analysis stage if required, since coverage probability on all 3
is the same (see section 7.2.1).   This assumes you are mostly interested in
estimating abundance in the forest as a whole.  Alternatively you could ignore
stratification altogether and allocate lines systematically throughout the study
area (rather than systematically within strata).

If you could potentially have far more lines per stratum then look at the
allocation formulae of section 7.2.2.3.

If you want to do stratified anlyses, but don't really have a good number of
lines per stratum (but do have more than 3!), you could consider estimating
spatial variation in encounter rate by estimating an overdispersion factor
common to all strata -- see formula 3.127 and text around that, and section
8.4.1 for a detailed example.

With your current data, given the small number of lines I think you should
regard the inferences you get as preliminary.  If your 3 strata are equal areas
then you have the same effort per stratum so you could try pooling strata to get
more reliable inference (although the CV will be high due to high variation in
encounter rate between lines).  Alternatively, you could try the overdispersion
method mentioned above.  Since you have so few detections in the low density
stratum you will have to estimate detection function pooled over strata -- this
will cause some bias if coverage probability is not even across strata.

Hope this helps,

 - Len

--

messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I am in the process of designing a survey for the arboreal southern muriqui
monkey, which inhabits the Atlantic forest of Brazil and whose grouping
patterns are best described as a 'loosely clumped spatial distribution of
individuals'.

However'clusters' of individuals do occur (with a variable cluster size) on
occasion, during aggregation in feeding trees and while sleeping.

My question is on what method of distance sampling is preferable in this
situation, when two forms of grouping patterns are likely? Does a survey of
one area have to maintain a standardised distance measurement, either
a)distance to each individual or b)cluster analysis or can two methods be
used within one survey, depending on the grouping pattern encountered? What
method is preferable?

Does anyone have experience surveying species with these characteristics or
on surveying mammals in tropical forests for further short discussions and
clarifications?

Thank you for your time,

messages.subject: Re: sampling loose clusters of primates
messages.body_plain:
Becky, for what it is worth, given I have no field experience with
monkeys, I would definitely record locations of individual monkeys when
they are in loose aggregations.  When they come together, provided you can
define this circumstance clearly (e.g. all animals within a circle of
radius xx m), I would record the centre of the cluster as the location,
and record the size of the cluster.  There is no difficulty in estimation
if you have different strategies for different types of cluster.  In fact,
you could opt to record individuals for both cluster types, if it is
practical to do that - the Distance methods are extremely robust to
failures of non-independence, and you should get very similar estimates
and variances either way.  The problem with recording loose aggregations
as clusters is that it is very difficult to estimate the 'centre of
gravity' of the cluster, and sometimes to estimate its size, and this can
introduce appreciable bias.

Steve Buckland

messages.body_plain:
Distance Group:

I have a dataset of point counts that I have analyzed in Distance.  I am
conducting preliminary power calculations of my abilities to detect
temporal trends from my data using program TRENDS.  An important factor
is whether the CV's vary in relation to abundance (1/vA) or are
independent of abundance.  In Statistical Guide to Data Analysis of
Avian Monitoring Programs (Nur, Jones, and Geupel 1999) the authors
suggest that for distance sampling, CV's would be independent of
abundance.  Would you agree and is this robust across species, for low
sample sizes, etc.?

I have a second question that has to do with binning.  I have found
using bins during analysis to be helpful in reducing the CV on density
estimates for some species, although I took the data using actual
distances rather than distance bands.  It appears as though my data are
suffering from heaping or movements away from observers.  We have heard
conflicting viewpoints on the validity in using bins in this context.
Furthermore, can comparisons be made among datasets collected in
different years if binning was helpful in one year but not in others?
In other words, if detection functions differ among years, then would it
be best to model each year differently and then compare the density
estimates, or lump the data and post-stratify by year?=20

Thank you very much,

> >
> > I have a dataset of point counts that I have analyzed in Distance.  I am
> > conducting preliminary power calculations of my abilities to detect
> > temporal trends from my data using program TRENDS.  An important factor
> > is whether the CV's vary in relation to abundance (1/vA) or are
> > independent of abundance.  In Statistical Guide to Data Analysis of
> > Avian Monitoring Programs (Nur, Jones, and Geupel 1999) the authors
> > suggest that for distance sampling, CV's would be independent of
> > abundance.  Would you agree and is this robust across species, for low
> > sample sizes, etc.?
> >

If I were doing it I would do both approaches and use the conservative
one that would suggest more sampling.  It is a tough call because it
will depend on what happens to the animal distribution as abundance
changes. Also some of it is under your control in that you can increase
effort if you find cv gets too large as abundance decreases. The std
error will often be proportional to abundance, so the cv will be
constant but that assumes distribution doesn't change.

> > I have a second question that has to do with binning.  I have found
> > using bins during analysis to be helpful in reducing the CV on density
> > estimates for some species, although I took the data using actual
> > distances rather than distance bands.  It appears as though my data are
> > suffering from heaping or movements away from observers.  We have heard
> > conflicting viewpoints on the validity in using bins in this context.
> > Furthermore, can comparisons be made among datasets collected in
> > different years if binning was helpful in one year but not in others?
> > In other words, if detection functions differ among years, then would it
> > be best to model each year differently and then compare the density
> > estimates, or lump the data and post-stratify by year?
> >

Data collection process and accuracy of your measurements should guide
your binning choice and not the cv of density. Unless your method of
measurement is changing from year to year, I would settle on a set of
bins and use for all years.  If you want to know whether you should pool
over years to estimate detectability, use AIC.  Fit all years separately
(different f(0) for each year) and sum AIC values and then compare that
to the AIC value for a single f(0) for all years combined. Better yet,
use year as a covariate in D4 (mcds engine). However there is a drawback
in using year as a covariate in D4 if you are using the hazard-rate.
Only the scale will vary and the exponent will be constant across
years.  If you are using the hazard rate, use the first approach of
separate fitting vs pooled fitting also.  If f(0) varies by year then
you should definitely fit separate f(0) to estimate annual
density/abundance.  Pooling robustness only guarantees that the average
abundance is ok pooling over factors (eg year).  It does not mean that
you'll get a useful estimate for any one of the factors (year). If f(0)
varies by year and you use a pooled f(0), some yearly estimates will be
biased. Some other warnings - you cannot compare AIC between binned and
unbinned analysis of the same data, nor can you compare AIC of the same
data set with different truncation widths.

--jeff laake

Tim Gerrodette wrote:
> >
> > Jeff,

> > I would like to comment on your response to the first part of the question,
> > the part that asks how CVs of estimates are related to abundance.  While other
> > methods of estimating abundance (eg, mark-recapture) may have other
> > relationships, in the case of distance sampling it is very likely that CVs
> > will be inversely related to abundance.  This can be seen heuristically by
> > considering the components of var(D):  cv(D)^2 = var(D)/D^2 = var(n)/n^2 +
> > var(f(0))/f(0)^2 + var(s)/s^2, where n is the number of observations and s is
> > group size.  Now consider how each of these 3 components is likely to change
> > as density, say, increases.  Given the same amount of survey effort, n will
> > increase as density increases.  We usually find that var(n)~a*n, where 1<a<3,
> > but the denominator is n*n, so var(n)/n^2 = cv(n)^2 decreases as density
> > increases.  f(0) and s probably don't change much as density increases
> > although, of course, more complicated scenarios are possible.  Larger sample
> > sizes, however, mean that estimates will generally improve - ie,  var(f(0))
> > and var(s) will decrease.  So it is likely that all 3 components of cv(D)^2,
> > and thus cv(D) itself, will decrease with increasing density.  Put the other
> > way around, as populations decrease in abundance, the precision of the
> > estimates of abundance, given the same effort, decreases.  This makes

messages.subject: ice on transect ?
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

what should one do if there is a varying amount of ice on the line
transect (e.g. boat-based), making specific but unknown transect areas
unavailable ?

Ideally, one could fly over the transect afterwards, take a picture of
the survey area, and subtract the iced area.
However, in reality that's usually impossible. Sometimes, ice floats
very fast, too, and modifies the image.

For now, I would treat surveys from such areas as underestimates since
the transect area assigned to corrected bird numbers is smaller than
what is used for the computation. I am unclear about the variance
though.

Thanks for any advice; best regards

    F.

I presume you mean that it is unuseable in the sense that D=0 in the
ice-covered areas.  If that is the case, you use the entire transect
length and the entire area of the survey region.  Average D will be
lower but with a proper design it will be unbiased for the entire region
and total abundance estimator will be unbiased.  However, the estimated
D is not an estimate of density in useable area, but is it really
necessary? It isn't needed to estimate abundance!

Now if what you are saying is that the critter is under the ice, then
you have a different problem.

--jeff

Aaron, I've pasted below text from the upcoming advanced distance sampling
book on pooling robustness.  (The book is now in press.)  Apologies for
the unreadable Latex'ed equations - but the text covers some of your
queries.

Steve

\section{Pooling robustness}
\label{ads_misc_pooling_robust}

Burnham {\it et al.}\ (1980) introduced the important concept of pooling
robustness.  They noted that detectability depends on many factors other
than just distance from the line or point. Some of these factors are
internal, such as age, sex or size of the animal, or cluster size if
animals occur in clusters. Others are external, such as weather,
visibility, habitat, observer or observation platform. Because data are
rarely adequate to allow stratification by more than one or two factors,
Burnham {\it et al.}\ (1980) note the importance of using models that
yield unbiased (or nearly unbiased) estimates when distance data collected
under variable conditions and on animals with varying intrinsic
detectabilities are pooled. We explore here the issue of pooling
robustness.

In Chapter \ref{ads_cov}, we provide methods that allow covariates to be
included in the model for detectability. These methods reduce the reliance
on pooling robustness, although they do not remove it altogether, as we
cannot be sure that we have the right covariates, entering our model in
the right form. The methods also allow the user to explore how
detectability varies as covariates vary. Another advantage of modelling
the covariates is when separate estimates are needed of different
components of the population, such as males and females. If we just pool
the data across the sexes when detectability varies by sex, pooling
robustness provides an estimate of total population size with low bias
(unless one sex is much more detectable than the other --- see below), but
the separate estimates of males and females may be appreciably
biased.  Addition of sex as a factor with two levels overcomes this
difficulty. However, the results of this section show that, if only an
overall abundance estimate is required, standard methods without
covariates are satisfactory under rather mild conditions, provided
heterogeneity in detectability is not too extreme.

Burnham {\it et al.}\ (1980: 45) consider partitioning line transect data
into $r$ strata, chosen so that there is little heterogeneity with each
stratum. The pooling robustness criterion is then defined as
\begin{equation}
\label{ach11_robust_criterion}
n\hat{f}(0) = \sum^r _{j=1} n_j \hat{f}_j(0)
\end{equation}
where $n_j$ is the number of detections in stratum $j$, $\hat{f}_j(0)$ is
the corresponding fitted pdf of distances of detected objects from the
line evaluated at zero distance, $n$ is the total number of detections,
and $\hat{f}(0)$ is the pdf fitted to the pooled distance data, evaluated
at zero distance.

In the following, we assume that animals occur singly; if they do not,
then each reference to `animal' below should be read as `cluster'.

Using the notation of Chapter \ref{ads_cov}, $y$ is distance from the line
or point, $\underline{z}$ are the covariates associated with an animal,
$g(y,\underline{z})$ is the probability of detection of an animal at
distance $y$ from the line or point and with covariate values
$\underline{z}$, and $f(y,\underline{z})$ is the corresponding joint
density function.

We make two key assumptions here:
\begin{enumerate}
\item{$g(0,\underline{z})=1$ for all $\underline{z}$}
\item{$\pi(y,\underline{z})=\pi(y)\pi(\underline{z})$, the product of the
marginals}
\end{enumerate}
Random line or point placement, or more usually random placement of a
systematic grid of lines or points, ensures independence of $y$ and
$\underline{z}$, so that the second assumption holds.

>From eqn (\ref{ach3_joint_density}),
\begin{equation}
f(y,\underline{z}) = \frac{g(y,\underline{z}) \, \pi(y) \,
\pi(\underline{z})}{\int\int g(y,\underline{z}) \,\pi(y) \,
\pi(\underline{z}) \, dy \, d\underline{z}}
\end{equation}

The marginal density of $y$ is therefore
\begin{equation}
f(y) = \frac{\int g(y,\underline{z}) \, \pi(y) \,
\pi(\underline{z})\,d\underline{z}}{\int\int
g(y,\underline{z}) \,\pi(y) \, \pi(\underline{z}) \, dy \, d\underline{z}}
\label{ach11_marginal}
\end{equation}

The probability that an animal at distance $y$ is detected, unconditional
on $\underline{z}$, is
\begin{equation}
g(y)=\int g(y,\underline{z})\,\pi(\underline{z})\, d\underline{z}
\end{equation}

Hence eqn (\ref{ach11_marginal}) simplifies to
\begin{equation}
f(y) = \frac{g(y) \, \pi(y)}{\int g(y) \,\pi(y) \, dy}
\end{equation}

For line transect sampling, given random line placement,
$\pi(y)=\frac{1}{w}$, so that
\begin{equation}
f(y) = \frac{g(y)}{\int g(y) \, dy}
\end{equation}
whereas for point transect sampling, we have $\pi(y)=\frac{2y}{w^2}$ and
\begin{equation}
f(y) = \frac{y\,g(y)}{\int y\,g(y) \, dy}
\end{equation}

These are exactly the results that apply in the absence of
heterogeneity. This is sufficient to show that the two sides of eqn
(\ref{ach11_robust_criterion}) have the same large-sample expectation; the
pooling robustness criterion can be assumed to hold provided we have a
sufficiently flexible model for $g(y)$ to fit to the observed distance
data.

The implications of these results are perhaps surprising. For example, the
training of shipboard observers often includes a warning that they should
maintain constant search effort. If observers search less efficiently in
areas of low density through boredom, and more efficiently when they are
in areas of high density, then the effective strip width is systematically
greater in high-density areas and less elsewhere. This was thought to
generate bias in abundance estimates, whereas the above results show that
it does not --- so long as they maintain $g(0)=1$ in both high and low
density areas. We would like observers to search with high efficiency
throughout, as a larger number of detections gives higher precision, but
abundance estimation is not compromised if efficiency is variable.

In Section \ref{ach11_cont_hr_models}, the hazard-rate model
$g(y)=1-exp[-(y/\sigma)^{-b}]$ was derived from homogeneous models for the
sighting process. In Fig.\ 11.2, composite detection functions were shown
when there is heterogeneity in detection probabilities. Although the
hazard-rate detection function has a
flat shoulder followed by a steep fall-off, the composite detection
function has a rounded
shoulder, more like that of the half-normal model. This illustrates that,
to utilize the model-robustness properties of line transect estimators, it
is important to use flexible models that can change shape when data
arising from different detection functions are pooled.

If heterogeneity is sufficiently extreme, it becomes difficult to model
adequately the detection function close to zero. For example in some
shipboard surveys, one or more observers search through $20\times$ or
$25\times$
binoculars, while another observer `guards the trackline' by searching
with the naked eye. If $g(0)$ is appreciably less than one for the main
observers, the detection function may appear to have a shoulder, but with
a spike of observations at around zero distance from the line (Fig.\ 2.1
of Buckland {\it et al}.\ (2001: 31)). Another example would be a species
of songbird, for which males are almost certain to be detected out to
perhaps 50 m or more, whereas females beyond perhaps 5 m may avoid
detection. This degree
of heterogeneity cannot be reliably modelled, resulting in bias.

Given assumption 1, that $g(0,\underline{z})=1$, then $g(0)=\int
g(0,\underline{z})\,\pi(\underline{z})\, d\underline{z} = 1$. If
$g(0,\underline{z})$ is a function of $\underline{z}$, then the model
robustness criterion fails, and we must model the heterogeneity to avoid
bias (Chapter \ref{ads_g(0)}).

Link (2003) noted the unidentifiability that can occur in estimating
population size using mark-recapture, when there is heterogeneity in the
capture probabilities. In the last sentence of that article, he stated
that `similar difficulties are to be anticipated in the use of distance
sampling models ..., in which inference is based on a density value at
zero.' The results of this section demonstrate that this is not true,
provided $g(0,\underline{z})=1$ for all $\underline{z}$. In
mark-recapture, to estimate population size, a model is needed that allows
estimation of the number of animals that are never caught, and different
models may give very different estimates. Mark-recapture data are discrete
counts of animals with different capture histories, and from these, we
must attempt to estimate the frequency of the `never caught' capture
history. By contrast, in line transect sampling, we seek to estimate
$f(0)$, the pdf of detection distances at zero distance, by fitting a
smooth, continuous function to $f(y)$. Under rather mild assumptions
(principally that $g(0,\underline{z})=1$ and that $g'(0,\underline{z})=0$
for all $\underline{z}$), the method works well. Similar arguments apply
in point transect sampling, where estimation of $h(0)$ relies on a good
model for the slope of the pdf at zero distance.

Falk, if there are no birds in the areas covered by ice, the problem is
simple in principle.  You can adopt 2 strategies.  In the first, you
simply exclude the ice covered areas, and treat it as a survey of the
remainder.  Then the density estimate is an estimate for areas without
ice.

In the second, you include areas covered by ice, include the effort you
would have expended, had you been able to survey the ice sections, and
assume that you would have recorded no birds on these sections.  In this
case, the density estimate is an average for the whole area, including
ice.

In either case, if you multiply the density estimate by the appropriate
area (without or with ice), you will get virtually the same abundance
estimate.

The second strategy does not need you to estimate what proportion of the
area is covered with ice.

A complication arises if survey effort is conducted when you are skirting
around the ice, on the way to the next section of ice-free transect.
If you include these data, you bias your estimates towards near-ice
densities.
